title: The Asian Dragon Puzzle: how multiple dispersal events have shaped the evolutionary history of Eastern Asian dragon pseudoscorpions (Arachnida: Pseudoscorpiones: Allochthonius)
content:
Abstract
East Asia is a biodiversity hotspot shaped by plate collisions, mountain orogeny, and sea-level fluctuations, yet evolutionary and biogeographical processes shaping East Asia’s endemic invertebrates remain poorly understood. We investigated these processes using Allochthonius pseudoscorpions, an ancient East Asian lineage serving as a proxy for leaf-litter invertebrates with limited dispersal abilities. Our dataset comprised 61 Allochthonius specimens representing 44 species-level units sampled from China, South Korea, Japan, and the Russian Far East, together with eight outgroup terminals and four molecular markers totalling 2550 bp. Phylogenetic analyses, divergence time estimation, and ancestral range reconstruction were used to examine historical biogeography and dispersal patterns. Allochthonius was recovered as monophyletic, with an estimated Early Cretaceous origin, and is now confined to East Asia, although an Eocene Baltic amber fossil indicates a formerly broader distribution. Divergence patterns reveal historical range shifts among Japan, the Korean Peninsula, and China associated with transient land connections from the Late Cretaceous to the Quaternary. Repeated faunal exchanges between the Korean Peninsula and the Japanese Archipelago indicate a complex history of dispersal and vicariance. Despite limited dispersal capacity, some lineages occur on both continental-shelf and volcanic islands. Collectively, these findings show that Allochthonius diversification reflects dynamic responses to repeated geographic connectivity, isolation, and habitat fragmentation from the Late Cretaceous to the Quaternary, highlighting the interplay of dispersal and vicariance in shaping biogeographical patterns of low-dispersal soil arthropods.
